item.title: What are Models?
item.description: A model is a representation of a real world system. In most cases, they are a simplification of this real world. Models are used extensively…
item.content:encoded:
A model is a representation of a real world system. In most cases, they are a simplification of this real world. Models are used extensively within all fields to better understand any system. Ranging from cosmic events to the model of an atom. Models also help us predict the behaviour and manipulate outcomes of systems. There are 2 components to the use of models, one is the academic aspect and the other is the application aspect.


Models can be mathematical. If the behaviour of a system can be represented by a set of parameters and the relation between these parameters can be deduced via experiments, natural observation, logical reasoning etc. Models can be more abstract than a set of equations. Models can be in the form of data in tables, like financial models in a spreadsheet. A flow chart can be used to represent a process and interaction between stages in a process. Models can be a block diagram that breaks down a system into its constituents and shows the relation and interaction between them. These kind of models are widely used within the realms of systems engineering. Thought processes and intuitive perception can be expressed using mental models. Mental models are just explanations of thought processes. In a nutshell, models can take a form of numbers, equations, diagrams or text.


What models are important?


The conscious human mind often can only give attention to one thing at a time. Even if we like to think that we are good at multi-tasking and handling multiple things at once, that is not true. However, it is said that our sub-conscious mind is capable of solving complex multi-variable multi-solution problems. This capability arises from spending a lot of time with that domain and giving enough training data to train your sub-conscious mind.


There are many examples where experts in fields could come to a solution for a complex problem based on an initial hunch or a gut-feeling. This is the subconscious mind at play. But the subconscious mind engages at its own will. If you go to bed thinking about a problem, there is a good chance that you have figured out something by the time you wake up. "Sleeping on it" is now a common idiom and there is some evidence that suggests that it works. This is a feat by the subconscious mind too. One way to engage the subconscious mind is to feed your conscious mind with information and knowledge about the domain and the problem that you are trying to solve. And to do this in a efficient way, we have to break down complex ideas and thoughts into a somewhat structured form. This will make it easier for the brain to chew on when we are not consciously thinking about it.


This makes it one of the most important reasons as to why we need more models that can explain complex events so that we can use our intelligence and build on top of it.


References


  • Centre for Advanced Spatial Analysis: Lecture 1

item.title: Autopiloting with Checklists
item.description: One prerequisite to be in a state of flow while working is to have good clarity on the goal and get immediate feedback. Being in such a…
item.content:encoded:
One prerequisite to be in a state of flow while working is to have good clarity on the goal and get immediate feedback. Being in such a state feels like you are on auto-pilot, you lose your perception of time and a feeling of calmness fill in you. Depending on the nature of the task, context and urgency you can convert parts of your workflow into chunks of flow-inducing work.


Another key aspect of being in a state of flow is that the tasks should be bordering on your existing capabilities making the task at hand challenging. Not too easy. Not too hard. Hence, tasks that fulfill the following characteristics would be ideal:


  • Repeatable on a high level but are nuanced each time
  • Recur over time
  • Hands-on nature
  • Require attention down to the details

Today's productivity apps like Todoist, Things all try to delight users with the satisfaction that they get when they check things off a list. In a small way, that too is immediate feedback to the user. A way for the user to see that they are progressing forward. This would make the format of a checklist more visual while doing a set of tasks.


Examples


  1. Colour grading: The goal is clear to the colorist, the kind of look that needs to be achieved is usually decided by a combination of color palettes and moodboards. The steps can be listed out even though all steps might not be needed for all clips. Each video clip is unique and requires you to focus on the tones and shades meticulously. Adjusting the dials to tweak exposure, saturation etc. are very hands-on.

  1. Standard surgical procedures: The goal of the procedure is clear. Standard procedures can be quantified as lists. There is a factor of uniqueness as each patient is different. And of course, very hands-on and requires high levels of focus. WHO has published a 19-point Surgical safety checklist aiming to decrease errors.

  1. Flight checks: Routine checks done by pilots before and after flights. Inherently very hands-on in nature. Repeatable and can be easily listed out. NASA published a paper that deeply looks into the concepts, design and use of cockpit checklists.


Taking it to the next level


There is another aspect to completing a checklist and that is how much time it would take. After doing a set of tasks a couple of times, you can probably estimate how much time you would need for doing the checklist once. Pre-scheduling blocks of time in your calendar based on your time estimate is a good way build it into your day without even thinking about it. Time boxing and scheduling can let you forget about these events and making time for it.


Get started


Here are some easy places where you can try to implement this:

  • Cleaning routine for your home
  • Cooking a dish by following a recipe
  • Pre-travel checklist
  • Monthly financial checks

item.title: Product-Market Fit in a Solution Space
item.description: Product-Market fit is a stage during the initial days of a startup when the product and users align. Sam Altman characterizes it as when the…
item.content:encoded:
Product-Market fit is a stage during the initial days of a startup when the product and users align. Sam Altman characterizes it as when the user start talking about your product to others on their own. Paul Graham's definition: Product market fit is when you build something that people want.


Startups take different time to achieve this depending on the problem it is trying to solve and the industry that it's in. Before a startup reaches product market fit, it will iterate through multiple solutions based on the feedback from different stakeholders. Shorter this feedback loop is, the "leaner" it is. The tricky part of achieving product-market fit is that it is a 2 dimensional problem. Each time you tweak the product, that in turn also shift the market for that new solution.


This journey until when the startup achieves product-market fit could be visualized as a 3 dimensional surface within a solution space for the problem that the startup is trying to solve. Any point on the surface is a feasible solution (simply meaning that it is valid and within physical and economic constraints), the closer this point is to the x-y plane, the closer it is to product-market fit. In this representation, a minima on the surface would be a natural point of equilibrium for a startup to reach. Startups would then need to traverse over this surface to find the minima, and the number of steps that it would take to reach will be the number of feedback loops that would be required. One solution space can have multiple minimums, the same way one problem can be solved in many ways. There exist different sets of decisions that would lead to these minimums over time. These different minimum could cater to different segments of the market. An easy example is Slack and Whatsapp. At it's core, they are both instant messaging apps but they are build, marketed and sold in a completed different way where the former is aimed to be a tool for the enterprise while the latter is part of an individual's social media presence.


Narrower the depression means fewer steps would be required to reach the minimum compared to a broader minimum. This doesn't necessarily mean the it is easier to reach product market fir if the depression is narrower. To better understand this, we need to understand what goes into each step that is traversed on the surface.


Fig 1: Visualization of a 3D surface and a possible path to it's minima.

Each step on the surface may include the following:

  • Customer Feedback
  • Data Harvesting and Analytics
  • Research Work
  • Engineering
  • Financial and Legal checks

Each step can be dependent on:

  • How the company is organised
  • Roadmap and vision
  • Economic Constraints

Key Takeaways


  1. The journey of a startup from ideation to product market fit can be visualised as a point on a 3d dimensional surface. A minima on this surface is an optimal solution, ie, product-market fit
  2. The characteristics of the surface are indicative of the nature of the industry and the problem that the startup is trying to solve
  3. There can exist multiple ways to achieve product-market fit within a solution space.

References


Fig 1 Image taken for illustrative purposes from: Oberndorfer, Christoph. (2017). Research on new Artificial Intelligence based Path Planning Algorithms with Focus on Autonomous Driving

item.title: Three Biases in the Market
item.description: The market seems to be reacting unsually well despite the rising numbers of COVID-19 cases. There are a combination of biases at play and…
item.content:encoded:
The market seems to be reacting unsually well despite the rising numbers of COVID-19 cases. There are a combination of biases at play and here are a few of them.




Confirmation Bias


Relief packages were announced by various government worldwide at the onset of the pandemic. This might have caused the market to reach positively initially. But the remainder of the recovery could be attributed to a very common bias known as confirmation bias. This bias make people believe certain things to be true simply because they want it to be true. When someone see's information that reinforces their existing beliefs, they are more prone to accept it than question it. This can lead to major blunders as it can turn a blind spot and hide from you the most common of gaps in a reasoning or an idea.


Opportunity Cost


The stock market might be the best of alternative compared to other options. Consumer spending trend has taken a hit due to the pandemic. Since eating out and travelling has mainly been put off, there is considerably less amount of spending in the past few months. This also means that market participants have more cash around. And having more of something can lead us to take more risks that we were unwilling to take otherwise. Since the 2008 financial crisis, there is an overall decreased trust in financial institutions. Especially in times like this when there is a higher chances of default. This can make the market participant be wary of the more complicated financial products altogether. Commodities are quite volatile during times like these and might not be a very easy option for most investors to allocate there money to. Relatively risk free options (like T-bills) doesn't seem that attractive either for an average investor. A lot of great companies are trading at a much lower price than its book value. This makes investing in stocks also quite attractive. Not to forget options like Vanguard which offers a piece of the economy over a long periods of time. And investing in a dip reduces the friction to put in your money for most participants.

Fear of missing out (FOMO)


For most people alive the 2008 financial crisis would be THE financial event that they have witnessed first hand. Movies like the big short have popularized and glamourized such events. News the hedge fund manager Bill Ackman made from betting on the eminent market dip also glamourizes it. Collectively this raises a feeling of FOMO among market participant. Nudging them even more and not letting them make the same mistakes in this dip. This could also have accelerated the market recovery despite the macro-economic situation.


Key Takeaways


  1. The market price is the collective reflection of the market participant's sentiment.
  2. This reflection is often a future average. Meaning that, to some degree it accounts for the events likely to happen in the future.
  3. The time window of the future average is quite short. ONe way to think about this is that if the market participants comprised majorly (like 80% or so) of long term investors, the future average would be indicative for a longer time window.

References


  • Confirmation Bias
  • Consumer Shopping WEF
  • Consumer Spending
  • Systemic Trust
  • Why commodities are volatile assets?
  • The Big Short
